facts.fact: Data Landscapers' 54-country review (an AI-assisted compilation, citing the DHIS2 Chad transition page) states that rural primary clinics record on paper registers, that aggregates are collated monthly and forwarded to district level where they are entered into DHIS2, and that 96% of districts were reporting directly into the system as of 2022.

Data Landscapers' review, citing a 2021 study in Massaguet district that included rural health centres, states that paper consultation registers and HMIS forms were in routine use and that data was digitised only at district level, using Excel, with paper stock-outs common.

Data Landscapers' review states that it found no evidence of routine digital entry or of DHIS2 at the point of care in rural clinics, and that plans for tablets for offline DHIS2 aggregate entry in northern regions had not been implemented widely; no date is given for the finding, so the date is the essay's publication date.
Data Landscapers' review, citing a 2021 study in Massaguet district, states that there was no EMR at clinics and that patient data was recorded in paper registers at the point of service.

Data Landscapers' review states that it found no evidence of an EMR at the point of care in rural clinics in Chad, where paper registers predominate; no date is given for the finding, so the date is the essay's publication date.

facts.fact: The Countdown to 2030 country team states that hospitals, which handle nearly half of deliveries, have reported weakly in recent years because their migration from the old health information system to DHIS2 is very slow and resisted by staff, that support to the hospitals has run since 2022 to complete the migration, and that the hospital reporting forms were revised at the end of 2023, delaying data entry.

The Countdown to 2030 country team reports facility reporting rates above 90% since 2020 and the share of districts whose monthly reports are at least 90% complete over a year rising from 78% in 2019 to 83% in 2023, with 2023 completeness held down by hospitals and by some hard-to-reach districts without internet coverage; it gives no share or count of health centres entering their own reports.

The Countdown to 2030 country team, meeting in April 2024, states that the country began integrating the data of private health facilities into its health information system (DHIS2) the previous December and that the process was still under way; private facilities' data had not been counted in earlier years.

facts.fact: The health ministry's PNDS 4 for 2022-2030, dated November 2022, names DHIS2 in its health information pillar: it sets the target of DHIS2 operational in all health districts by 2030, with districts using it synchronised and in real time rising from a baseline of 82% to 100%, and carries budget-coded actions to sustain DHIS2, extend it to districts left out of the initial plan and to health centres, and make it interoperable with the SIGL and the programme trackers.

PNDS 4 states that the ministry's Direction des Statistiques et du Système d'Information Sanitaire (DSSIS) is charged with running every part of the health information system, from designing the tools to producing the information, and describes DHIS2 as the new computerised system deployed with user training, equipment and a central server.

PNDS 4 states that data are collected daily in health facilities on primary tools (registers and forms) and compiled into monthly activity reports (RMA), refers to the entry of the RMA being decentralised to the health districts, and lists extending DHIS2 to the level of the health centres as an action still to be carried out.

PNDS 4 states that DHIS2 has been operational in all provinces since July 2022 and gives a baseline of 82% of health districts using it synchronised and in real time, without numerator or denominator; it publishes no share or count of health centres entering their own reports.

facts.fact: Moukénet and colleagues (BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making) state that in Chad HMIS data are collected by health facilities on paper forms, checked by the facility manager and reported to the health district, where the zonal chief or district manager converts the data of health facilities and district hospitals to electronic format in Microsoft Excel and sends them by email or flash key to the provincial delegation and then the ministry; the description is undated and is placed at the article's publication year.

Moukénet and colleagues describe reporting at health-centre level as paper-based throughout, with stock-outs of register books at 37.5% and of HMIS forms at 12.5% of the 16 health centres of Massaguet district during 2018, and recommend moving from paper forms to a web-based HMIS; no health centre is described as entering its own data.

Moukénet and colleagues state that health centres and district hospitals report monthly into the HMIS on paper, and measured reporting completeness of 95.24% (CI 90.83-97.92) in the HMIS data of 14 government-recognised health centres in Massaguet district for January-December 2018, with attendance and malaria cases over-reported against the registers (verification factors 1.41 to 2.86).

Moukénet and colleagues state that HMIS data end at the health ministry's Department of Statistics and Health Information (SDSIS), which verifies their consistency at central level and supervises districts and health centres with the malaria programme and the provincial delegation; the description is undated and is placed at the article's publication year.
